title: Casting Directors Are Finally Getting Their Moment — Here's Why It Matters for Talent
excerpt: From a historic Oscar nomination to big wins at the CDG Casting Awards, casting directors are getting more recognition than ever — here's what that means for actors and models seeking representation.
content:
For years, casting directors have been the invisible architects behind some of the best performances on screen — spotting the actor nobody else saw, matching faces to roles with an instinct that can make or break a production. This year, that work is finally being recognised at the highest level.

British casting director Nina Gold has made history as the first UK nominee for the newly created Academy Award for Best Casting, recognised for her work on Hamnet. It's a milestone moment: an entirely new Oscar category, and a British casting director leading the pack in its inaugural year.

Meanwhile, at the CDG Casting Awards 2026, Shaheen Baig and Rachel Sheridan each walked away with two wins, including Best Child Casting and Best Casting for a Limited or Single Series for their work on Adolescence — one of the most talked-about series of the year. Lauren Evans also picked up Best Casting for an Independent Film for I Swear, which went on to receive five BAFTA nominations.

## Why This Matters Beyond the Awards

For actors, models, and performers, this shift in recognition isn't just industry trivia — it reflects something real about how the business works:

Casting is a craft, not a formality. The people making these decisions are being celebrated precisely because they take the process seriously — reading rooms, chemistry, range, not just headshots.

Strong casting elevates strong material. Productions like Adolescence and Hamnet are proof that the right casting choices can be the difference between a good project and an unforgettable one.

The industry is paying closer attention to process. As casting gets more institutional recognition, the standards and expectations placed on talent — preparation, professionalism, tape quality — are only going to rise.

## What This Means If You're Looking for Representation

At Next Stage Talent, this is exactly the environment we prepare our talent for. We work on a commission-only basis — no upfront fees, ever — because our success is tied directly to yours. Understanding what casting directors are actually looking for, and helping you show up ready for it, is the whole point of what we do.

If awards season is teaching us anything this year, it's that the industry is investing more seriously in the casting process than ever. That's good news for performers who take their craft seriously too.

title: The Biggest Misconception About Getting Signed: You Don't Need Photos or a Showreel Yet
excerpt: Think you can sort your photos and reel out after you sign with an agency? Here's why that thinking holds talent back — and what actually gets you noticed.
content:
One of the most common things we hear from new and aspiring talent is some version of: "I'll sort out proper photos and a showreel once I get signed."

It's an understandable assumption — but it has the process backwards, and it's one of the biggest reasons promising talent gets overlooked before they even get a fair look.

## Why This Misconception Exists

Signing with an agency can feel like the starting line, so it makes sense to assume the agency will help build your materials from scratch afterward. In reality, agencies — and more importantly, casting directors — are making fast judgment calls based on what they can see right now. Representation doesn't create your marketability from nothing; it amplifies what's already there.

## What Photos and a Showreel Actually Do

Photos are your first filter. Before anyone reads a bio or watches a tape, a casting director or agent is scanning headshots. Poor quality, outdated, or overly filtered photos get skipped in seconds — regardless of talent.

A showreel proves range, not just looks. Photos show who you are; a reel shows what you can do — how you move, deliver a line, hold the camera's attention. Without it, agents are being asked to represent a guess.

They signal that you're serious. Turning up with professional (not necessarily expensive) materials tells an agency you understand the industry is a business, not just a hobby.

## What "Professional" Actually Requires

You don't need a Hollywood budget to get this right.

Photos: Natural light, simple background, around 30 to 40 photos showing real variety — different outfits, expressions, angles, and settings — with minimal editing. Clarity and honesty matter more than polish — the photos need to look like you on a normal day, not a heavily retouched version.

Showreel: Even 60–90 seconds of well-shot, well-edited footage showing 2–3 different tones (e.g. comedic, dramatic, natural) is more useful than five minutes of unfocused clips. If you don't have prior footage, self-tapes done properly can serve the same purpose early on.

## Where This Fits Into Getting Signed

At Next Stage Talent, we work on a commission-only basis — we only succeed when you book work — so we're upfront about what actually gets you seen. Coming to us with even simple, honest photos and a short reel puts you miles ahead of someone waiting for representation to "figure it out" for them.

The takeaway: don't wait for an agency to justify investing in your materials — invest in materials that make an agency want to represent you.

title: Inside the Spotlight Prize 2026: Meet the Next Generation of UK Talent
excerpt: The Spotlight Prize 2026 brought together 40 finalists from 60 UK and Ireland drama schools — here's what happened, who won, and why it matters for emerging talent.
content:
Every year, the Spotlight Prize brings together the most promising graduating performers from across the UK and Ireland, giving them a rare shot at performing directly in front of the casting directors, agents, and producers who shape the industry. The 2026 edition just wrapped, and it was one of the biggest yet.

A Record Year for Finalists

This year's showcase featured an expanded format, with 40 finalists split across two categories: the Screen Prize and the Stage Prize. Twenty schools were represented in each category, with only a handful of schools landing finalists in both — a reminder of just how competitive the selection process is, drawing nominees from over 60 drama schools and universities.

The Screen Prize finalists recorded monologues at Spotlight's studios under the direction of Paulette Randall MBE, while the Stage Prize finalists performed live in front of an invited industry audience, directed by actor and Open Door founder David Mumeni.

The Results

After a night of performances in London, the judging panels faced tough decisions. The Screen Prize went to Molly McLoughlin from The Lir. The Stage Prize category saw such a close call between two standout performances that the jury made the rare decision to award two joint winners — one for spoken word, one for musical performance.

Why This Matters

The Spotlight Prize has a track record of launching serious careers — past finalists include Dame Judi Dench, Brian Cox, Jim Broadbent, and Ben Whishaw. For every performer competing this year, simply reaching the finals put them in front of exactly the kind of industry attention that can define the next stage of a career.

For anyone earlier in their journey, this is a good reminder of what the ladder looks like: showcases like this exist precisely to connect fresh talent with the people making casting decisions. Whether or not you've walked that particular stage, the underlying lesson holds — visibility in front of the right people, at the right moment, is what turns potential into opportunity.

title: How to Prepare for Your First Casting Call
excerpt: SHORT EXCERPT: Nervous about your first casting call? Here's what to actually bring, wear, and expect — plus the common mistakes that trip up first-timers.
content:
Your first casting call can feel like a huge unknown. The good news: casting directors aren't looking to catch you out — they're looking for reasons to remember you. A little preparation goes a long way toward making that happen.

Before You Go

Read the brief properly. Know the project, the role, and what's being asked of you (a scene, a monologue, an improvisation). Turning up without having read the brief is one of the fastest ways to stand out for the wrong reasons.

Prepare, don't over-rehearse. You want to know your material well enough to be flexible in the room — not so rigidly rehearsed that you can't take direction if they ask you to try it differently.

What to Bring
A printed headshot and CV, even if you've already submitted digitally
A notebook and pen
Any specific items requested in the brief (a prop, a particular style of clothing)
Water and a snack — casting days often involve waiting
What to Wear

Dress to suggest the character, not to costume as them. If you're auditioning for a corporate role, smart-casual works better than a full suit. If it's a young parent role, dress like a real person who might have that life — avoid literal costumes.

In the Room

Be polite to everyone, not just the casting director — assistants and readers often have more influence on the process than people expect. Listen to any direction given before your take and be ready to adjust. If something goes wrong (you trip on a line, a phone goes off), stay composed — casting directors have seen it all and care more about how you recover than whether it happened.

Common First-Timer Mistakes
Arriving without knowing the exact time and location, leading to a rushed entrance
Over-apologising throughout the audition
Treating the reader (the person feeding you lines) as an afterthought rather than a scene partner
Leaving immediately after the audition instead of thanking the room
The Takeaway

Casting calls reward preparation and calm more than perfection. Go in knowing your material, dressed appropriately, and ready to be flexible — the rest comes with experience.

title: Self-Tapes Done Right: A Beginner's Guide
excerpt: Self-tapes have become the default first round for most auditions. Here's how to get lighting, framing, sound, and slating right — without needing a professional studio.
content:
Self-tapes are now the first step in most casting processes, which means your ability to shoot a clean, professional-looking tape at home is just as important as your performance itself. The good news: you don't need expensive equipment to get this right — you need to understand what actually matters.

Lighting

Natural daylight from a window facing you is usually your best option — position yourself facing the light, not with it behind you. Avoid overhead lighting that casts shadows under your eyes. If natural light isn't available, a simple ring light or even a desk lamp with a diffuser (a white sheet or paper works fine) can do the job.

Framing

Frame from the chest up for most auditions unless the brief says otherwise. Keep your eyeline just off-camera, at the height of the lens, and make sure the camera is stable — a tripod or a stack of books works better than handheld.

Sound

Sound quality often matters more than picture quality. Film in a quiet room, away from traffic noise, humming appliances, or echoey spaces. A basic clip-on microphone or even wired headphones with a mic can dramatically improve audio over a phone's built-in microphone.

Background

Keep it simple and neutral — a plain wall or curtain works. Avoid busy backgrounds, personal clutter, or anything that pulls focus from your performance.

Slating

Most briefs will ask for a short slate at the start: your name, your agency (if any), your height, and sometimes your location. Keep it brief, natural, and confident — this is often the first impression a casting director gets of you, so treat it as part of the performance, not just admin.

Common Mistakes to Avoid
Filming in portrait orientation instead of landscape
Reading directly off a script visible in frame instead of learning the lines
Multiple uncut takes bundled into one file instead of your best, clearly labelled take
Poor file naming that makes it hard for casting to find your tape (always include your name)
The Takeaway

A self-tape doesn't need to look expensive — it needs to look intentional. Good lighting, clear sound, and a stable frame let your performance do the work, which is exactly what casting directors are trying to evaluate.

At Next Stage Talent, we help our talent get self-tape ready, because more often than not, that tape is the only shot you get before the room.

title: Casting Director Advice: What They Really Look For
excerpt: We've pulled together advice shared publicly by leading casting directors — the honest, straight-talking tips that could make a real difference to your next audition.
content:
Casting directors see hundreds of faces every week. They know within seconds whether someone has what they're looking for. So what are they actually looking for? Here's what they've said publicly — in their own words.

## "Just Be Yourself"

One of the most repeated pieces of advice from casting directors is simple: don't try to act anything. Be yourself. Authenticity is immediately obvious on camera, and so is the lack of it.

Casting directors consistently say that the talent who try too hard to be what they think the room wants end up blending into the crowd. The ones who walk in confident and genuine are the ones who get remembered.

## "Make Bold Choices"

Playing it safe is the fastest way to be forgotten. Leading casting directors encourage talent to make bold, committed choices — whether it's in how they deliver a line, how they hold themselves, or how they interpret a brief.

The best audition of your career won't necessarily get you the job, but a reputation for auditioning well will lead to more opportunities and more chances to shine.

## "Never Tell a Lie"

Honesty matters more than you might think. If they ask whether you can horse-ride and you can't, say so. Being caught in a lie on set is far more damaging than admitting your limitations up front.

## "Keep It Simple"

When it comes to headshots and portfolios, casting directors are clear: stop trying so hard. Clean, natural, up-to-date imagery will always outperform over-produced alternatives.

## "Prepare Like You Mean It"

If you've been given a brief or a script in advance, know it cold. The talent who come in prepared stand out immediately.

At Next Stage Talent, we make sure our talent are briefed properly before every casting — so they walk in knowing exactly what to expect and how to present themselves at their best.

title: How to Stand Out at a Commercial Casting
excerpt: Commercial castings are different from acting auditions. Here's what casting directors and industry insiders say you need to do to get noticed — and booked.
content:
Commercial castings are fast-paced and competitive. The casting director might see fifty people in a single afternoon. Here's how to make sure you're the one they remember.

## Dress Simply

Wear simple, well-fitted clothing. Avoid busy patterns, large logos, or anything too distracting. The casting director needs to be able to visualise you representing a brand.

## Be a Good Listener

One of the most underrated skills in a casting is the ability to listen. Follow direction without trying to add your own interpretation until invited to. The talent who listen carefully and respond naturally are the ones who get called back.

## Your Portfolio Should Start Strong

Lead with strong beauty shots and headshots that highlight your natural features, followed by full-length images showing range. For commercial work, include shots in everyday, relatable settings.

## Build Relationships, Not Just a CV

Every casting, even one you don't book, is an opportunity to be remembered positively. A reputation for being professional, easy to work with, and reliable is worth more than any single job.

## Embrace Modern Formats

Self-tape auditions and virtual castings are now standard. Good lighting, a clean background, clear audio — a well-produced self-tape immediately sets you apart.

title: What Brands Look for When Casting Commercial Models
excerpt: Commercial modelling is one of the most accessible and rewarding areas of the industry. But what exactly are brands looking for? Here's what casting directors tell us again and again.
content:
Commercial modelling is different from high fashion. It's about real people, relatable faces, and the ability to connect with an audience. And that means the qualities brands look for might surprise you.

## Authenticity Over Perfection

Commercial clients are not looking for flawless runway models. They want people who look real, approachable, and genuine. If you can smile naturally in front of a camera and make a product feel like part of everyday life, you have exactly what most commercial brands need.

## Versatility

The most successful commercial models can adapt. They can be professional one moment and fun the next. They take direction well and can shift their energy depending on what the shoot requires.

## A Strong, Up-to-Date Portfolio

Your portfolio is the first thing a casting director will look at. It should show range — different looks, expressions, and scenarios. Make sure your photos are recent and reflect how you look today.

## Reliability and Professionalism

Brands work to tight schedules. Showing up on time, prepared, and with a positive attitude is non-negotiable. Casting directors remember the talent who make their jobs easy — and recommend them again and again.

## The Right Measurements — But Not What You Think

Commercial modelling has far broader size and age requirements than fashion modelling. Brands want to represent their actual customers, which means there are opportunities for all shapes, sizes, and ages.

## How Next Stage Talent Can Help

title: How to Build a Modelling Portfolio That Gets You Noticed
excerpt: Your portfolio is your most important tool as a model. Here's exactly what to include, what to avoid, and how to make sure it stands out to casting directors and agencies.
content:
A strong modelling portfolio can open doors. A weak one can close them before you've even had a chance to speak. Here's how to make sure yours does the right job.

## Quality Over Quantity

You don't need fifty photos. You need ten to fifteen excellent ones. Casting directors look at hundreds of portfolios — they will notice immediately if yours is padded with filler shots.

Choose images that are sharp, well-lit, and show you at your best. If you only have a few truly great photos, use those and keep adding as your career develops.

## Show Range

Variety is essential. Your portfolio should include a mix of close-up headshots, three-quarter shots, and full-length images. Show different expressions — not just smiling. If you can, include shots in different settings and outfits.

## Keep It Current

Your portfolio should look like you do today. If your hair is completely different or your photos are more than two years old, it's time for new ones. Nothing undermines trust faster than turning up to a casting looking nothing like your portfolio.

## Simple Is Better

Avoid heavy retouching, overly dramatic lighting, or distracting backgrounds. Casting directors want to see your face, your proportions, and your personality — not a heavily edited version of you.

## Include a Comp Card

A composite card (or comp card) is a single sheet with your key stats and a selection of your best photos. Most agencies and casting directors expect to receive one. At Next Stage Talent, we advise all our talent on what to include.

## Work With a Professional Photographer

If you're serious about your career, invest in professional photos. A good photographer who specialises in modelling portfolios will know exactly what casting directors are looking for.

Not sure where to start? Our team at Next Stage Talent can advise on the right approach for your specific goals and the type of work you want to pursue.

title: The Difference Between a Talent Agent and a Casting Agency
excerpt: Many people use the terms interchangeably, but a talent agent and a casting agency do very different things. Understanding the difference could be important for your career.
content:
If you're new to the modelling and acting industry, the terminology can be confusing. Talent agents, casting agencies, model agencies, management companies — what does it all mean? Here's a clear breakdown.

## What a Talent Agent Does

A talent agent represents individual talent. Their job is to find work for the people they represent — submitting them for roles, negotiating contracts on their behalf, and developing their careers over time.

At Next Stage Talent, this is what we do. We are a talent agency. Our clients are the models, actors, and commercial talent we represent. We work for them.

## What a Casting Agency Does

A casting agency works on the other side of the table. They are hired by brands, film studios, and production companies to find the right talent for a specific project. They don't represent talent — they source it.

When a brand needs models for a TV commercial, they might hire a casting director to find them. That casting director will then reach out to talent agencies like Next Stage Talent to submit suitable people.

## Why This Matters

Understanding this difference helps you know who is working for you and who is working for the client.

A talent agent earns a percentage of the work they secure for you. This means their success is directly linked to yours.

## Next Stage Talent: Your Agent

We are a talent agency — which means we are on your side. Our job is to represent you, promote you, and find you work. Every submission we make, every relationship we build with casting directors, is done with your career in mind.

If you're looking for an agent who will genuinely work for you, we'd love to talk.

title: How Social Media Can Help Your Modelling Career in 2026
excerpt: Social media has changed the way models get discovered, noticed, and booked. Here's how to use it properly to support your career — without making the mistakes that hold people back.
content:
Social media is now one of the most powerful tools a model can have — but only if you use it the right way. Here's what actually works in 2026.

 Casting Directors Check Your Profile

Before responding to a submission, most casting directors and brand managers will look at your social media. And here's the important part — they're not looking at your follower count. They're looking at how you present yourself. Is your profile clean and professional? Do your photos show consistency? Do you come across as someone a brand would want to work with?

 Quality Over Quantity

The models who get noticed are not necessarily the ones who post every day. They're the ones who post consistently well. Three to five quality posts per week is far more effective than daily content that isn't thought through.

 Keep Your Bio Simple and Professional

Your bio should make it immediately clear who you are and what you do. Include that you're represented by Next Stage Talent — it adds credibility and shows casting directors you're serious about your career.

Caption Smart

Short, professional captions work best in the casting environment. Credit the photographer, the brand, or the location where relevant. This shows industry awareness and builds relationships with the people you work with.

What to Avoid

Avoid anything that could put a brand off — controversial opinions, unprofessional photos, or anything that contradicts the image you're trying to build. Your social media is your public portfolio. Treat it that way.

Let Your Agent Help

At Next Stage Talent, we advise our talent on how to position themselves online. If you're unsure whether your profile is working for or against you, ask us. A few small changes can make a significant difference to the opportunities that come your way.

title: The Truth About Getting Signed to a Talent Agency
excerpt: There's a lot of confusion — and misinformation — about how talent agencies work, how to get signed, and what to expect once you are. Here's the honest version.
content:
Self-tapes are now the standard first step in almost every casting process — for commercial work, TV, film, and beyond. A well-produced self-tape can get you through to the next round. A poor one will cost you the opportunity, no matter how talented you are.

Here's exactly how to get it right.

## Set Up Your Background

Use a plain, neutral background — a clean wall, a door, or a simple backdrop. Avoid busy rooms, cluttered shelves, or anything that distracts from you. Casting directors are watching you, not your living room.

If you don't have a plain wall, hang a plain bedsheet. It doesn't need to be expensive. It needs to be clean and simple.

## Get Your Lighting Right

Natural light from a window in front of you is ideal. If you're shooting in the evening or in a dark room, invest in a basic ring light — they cost very little and make a significant difference.

Never shoot with the light source behind you. You'll appear as a silhouette and casting directors won't be able to see your face.

## Sound Matters More Than You Think

Poor audio is one of the most common reasons self-tapes get skipped. If your voice is muffled, echoing, or competing with background noise, the casting director will move on.

Record in a quiet room. If you have earphones with a built-in microphone, use them. Or invest in a basic clip-on microphone — again, inexpensive and worth every penny.

## Frame Yourself Correctly

Your face and upper body should fill the frame. Position the camera at eye level — not above or below. Prop your phone on a stack of books if needed. Looking slightly up or down at the camera reads badly on screen.

## Know Your Material

If you've been sent a script or brief, know it thoroughly before you record. Looking down at notes kills the performance. If you need an eye-line for another character, place a mark on the wall just next to the camera lens.

## Record Multiple Takes

Record at least three takes and choose the best one. Don't settle for the first acceptable version — watch it back critically and ask yourself honestly whether it represents your best work.

title: What to Wear to a Casting — and What to Avoid
excerpt: What you wear to a casting tells a casting director a lot before you've said a word. Here's how to get it right every time.
content:
What you wear to a casting tells a casting director a lot before you've said a word. It's not about fashion — it's about making their job easier. Here's how to get it right every time.

## The Golden Rule: Simple Always Wins

Your outfit should never distract from you. Busy patterns, large logos, bold slogans, and anything overly trendy can pull focus away from your face and personality — which is what casting directors are actually there to assess.

Stick to plain, well-fitted clothing in neutral or solid colours. Navy, grey, white, black, and soft tones all work well. They photograph cleanly and help your face become the focal point.

## Fit Matters More Than Brand

An expensive outfit that doesn't fit well will always look worse than a simple, inexpensive piece that fits perfectly. Casting directors notice fit. Clothes that are too baggy hide your proportions; clothes that are too tight look uncomfortable.

If you're going for commercial modelling work specifically, wear something that looks like a real person's wardrobe — because that's exactly what brands are casting for.

## Consider the Brief

If you've been given a brief or a character description in advance, let it inform your outfit choice — but don't go overboard. A hint in the right direction is enough. If the role is corporate, wear something clean and professional. If it's lifestyle or casual, dress accordingly.

When in doubt, smart casual is almost always appropriate.

## What to Avoid

Avoid anything that could cause problems on camera — reflective fabrics, very fine stripes (which can create a strobing effect), hats that cast shadows on your face, and heavy jewellery that jangles or distracts.

Also avoid wearing something you're uncomfortable in. If you're tugging at your hem or adjusting your collar throughout the casting, it will show.

## Grooming Is Part of the Outfit

Come to a casting looking like you've made an effort — clean hair, clean nails, minimal fragrance. You don't need heavy makeup or an elaborate hairstyle. Natural and polished is the standard.

## At Next Stage Talent

Before every casting, we brief our talent on what to wear based on the specific brief. You'll never go into a room unprepared when you're represented by us.

title: Is Background and Extras Work Worth It?
excerpt: Background and extras work is often the first step into the industry for new talent. But is it worth your time? Here's an honest breakdown.
content:
Background and extras work is often the first step into the industry for new talent. It gets you on set, earns you a credit, and gives you a feel for how professional productions run. But is it worth your time? Here's an honest breakdown.

## What Is Background Work?

Background artists — sometimes called extras — appear in the background of film, TV, and commercial productions. You might be a customer in a coffee shop scene, a pedestrian on a busy street, or a guest at a party. You're not the focus, but you're essential to making a scene feel real.

## What You'll Learn On Set

For someone new to the industry, background work is genuinely educational. You'll learn how a professional set operates — the hierarchy, the pace, the terminology, the etiquette. You'll understand what a first assistant director does, how takes work, how long things actually take.

That knowledge is invaluable when you step into a more prominent role. Talent who have background experience tend to be more relaxed and professional on set because they've already seen how it all works.

## The Pay

Background work is paid, though rates vary depending on the production, the union status, and the hours. It's rarely life-changing money, but it's legitimate industry income. Check rates carefully before committing to any booking.

## The Limitations

Background work is not a stepping stone to principal roles in the way people sometimes hope. Casting directors for speaking roles rarely pick from the background cast. The two paths are largely separate.

It also requires a lot of patience — you may spend long hours waiting on set for a short amount of screen time.

## When It Makes Sense

Background work makes most sense early in your career, when you want to build experience and confidence on set. It can also be useful for filling gaps between other work and for building up your industry contacts.

It makes less sense as your primary focus once you've established yourself, because the time investment can take you away from pursuing principal roles and modelling work.

We work with talent across a range of levels — from those just starting out to those with significant credits. If you're interested in exploring background work as part of your early career, we can advise on whether it's the right move for you.

title: How to Handle Rejection in the Modelling and Acting Industry
excerpt: Rejection is part of the job. Every working model and actor has been turned down more times than they've been booked. Here's how to handle it in a way that actually helps your career.
content:
Rejection is part of the job. Every working model and actor — no matter how successful — has been turned down far more times than they've been booked. The difference between those who build lasting careers and those who don't isn't talent alone. It's how they handle not getting the job.

## It Is Almost Never Personal

The most important thing to understand about rejection in this industry is that it is almost never about you as a person. Casting decisions are made based on dozens of factors — brief requirements, brand guidelines, what other talent looks like, what the director had in mind that morning.

You could be exactly right for a job and still not get it because someone else was slightly more right. That's not failure. It's the nature of the work.

## Don't Seek Feedback After Every Rejection

It's natural to want to know why you didn't get the job. But casting directors rarely have time to give detailed feedback, and asking repeatedly can leave a negative impression. Focus on what you can control — your preparation, your professionalism, your portfolio — rather than analysing every decision that goes against you.

## Keep Going to Castings

The single best response to rejection is to keep showing up. Every casting is practice. Every room you walk into builds your confidence and your reputation for being someone who takes their career seriously. Casting directors remember the talent who come back again and again — professionally, without bitterness.

## Look After Your Mental Health

The industry can be tough on your sense of self-worth. It's important to maintain a clear separation between your value as a person and your success rate at castings. Your identity is not your booking rate.

Talk to people you trust. Take breaks when you need them. And remember that even the most in-demand talent have slow periods.

## Use Quiet Periods Productively

When the castings aren't coming in and the bookings are slow, use the time. Update your portfolio. Work on your self-tape setup. Take a class. Build relationships. The groundwork you lay during quiet periods often determines how quickly things pick up.

## At Next Stage Talent

We support our talent through the difficult patches, not just the successes. If you're finding it tough, your agent is there to talk to — not just to submit you for work, but to help you navigate the career as a whole.

title: How to Write a Model Application That Actually Gets Read
excerpt: Most model applications say the same things. Here's how to write one that stands out — and gives an agency exactly what they need to make a decision.
content:
Most model applications say the same things. "I've always wanted to model." "People tell me I have a good look." "I'm hardworking and dedicated." These phrases appear in hundreds of applications every week and tell an agency almost nothing useful.

Here's how to write one that actually stands out.

## Keep It Short

Agencies receive a lot of applications. A long, rambling email is less likely to be read carefully than a short, clear one. Three to four sentences is enough for an initial application. Say who you are, what you're looking for, and why you're contacting this agency specifically. Then let your photos do the rest.

## Give the Practical Information First

Before anything else, include your name, age, location, and key measurements or stats. Agencies need this information to assess whether you're suitable for the type of work they handle. If you make them dig for it, you're making their job harder.

## Be Honest About Your Experience

If you have no experience, say so clearly. Pretending otherwise always comes out. Agencies are not put off by inexperience — they're put off by dishonesty. A genuine, well-presented new face is far more appealing than someone who has exaggerated their background.

If you do have experience, list it briefly and factually. Credits, campaigns, any reputable work you've done. Keep it relevant.

## Attach the Right Photos

Include two to four photos — a clear headshot, a natural smiling shot, and one or two full-length images. These should be recent, well-lit, and show you as you actually look. No heavy filters, no dramatic poses, no photos taken in poor light.

If you have professional photos, use them. If not, a good-quality phone photo in natural daylight is perfectly acceptable for an initial application.

## Don't Ask for Feedback if You're Rejected

If an agency doesn't respond or declines, don't reply asking for a detailed critique. It's unlikely to result in useful feedback and can leave a poor impression. Move on and try elsewhere. The right agency will respond when the time is right.

title: What Actually Happens on a Commercial Shoot Day
excerpt: If you've never been on a commercial shoot before, you might not know what to expect. Here's a realistic look at what a typical shoot day involves — from call time to wrap.
content:
If you've never been on a commercial shoot before, the whole thing can feel mysterious. Here's a realistic look at what a typical shoot day involves — so you go in prepared, not surprised.

## The Call Time

You'll be given a call time — the time you need to arrive on set. This is not a suggestion. Arriving late to a shoot is one of the fastest ways to damage your reputation in the industry. Build in extra time for travel, and always confirm the exact location the day before.

Call times for commercial shoots are often early. Six or seven in the morning is not unusual, particularly for outdoor shoots that rely on specific light.

## Arrival and Check-In

When you arrive, you'll typically check in with a runner or production coordinator. You may need to sign a contract or release form if you haven't already done so in advance. Read anything you sign carefully.

## Hair, Makeup, and Wardrobe

Most commercial shoots have a hair and makeup artist and a wardrobe stylist on set. You'll be taken through these before you go in front of the camera. This process can take anywhere from twenty minutes to well over an hour depending on the look required.

Arrive with clean hair and a clean face unless you've been specifically asked to come with makeup done. Bring any personal items the stylist has requested — specific underwear, shoe size, anything mentioned in the brief.

## Waiting

Here is the part nobody tells you about: commercial shoots involve a lot of waiting. Sets are complex operations and things rarely run exactly to schedule. You may wait for lighting to be adjusted, for another talent to finish, for a director decision to be made.

Come prepared. Bring something to read, headphones, a snack. Stay calm, stay pleasant, and don't show impatience. The way you behave between takes is noticed.

## On Camera

When it's your turn, you'll receive direction from the director or first assistant director. Listen carefully, respond quickly, and don't be afraid to ask for clarification if you're unsure what's being asked of you.

You'll likely do multiple takes. Don't assume a take was bad just because they go again — directors almost always shoot multiple versions for the edit.

## Wrap

When the shoot wraps, thank the team, collect any personal items from wardrobe, and leave promptly. A professional attitude at the end of the day is just as important as one at the beginning.

## At Next Stage Talent

We prepare our talent for every shoot they go to. You'll know what to expect, what to bring, and how to conduct yourself before you ever arrive on set.

title: How to Use Instagram to Get Noticed by a Talent Agency
excerpt: Instagram has become one of the most effective tools for models and actors looking to get spotted. But most people use it wrong. Here's how to make your profile work for your career.
content:
Instagram has become one of the most effective tools for aspiring models and actors — but most people use it in ways that actively work against them. Here's how to make your profile work for your career.

## Think of It as a Portfolio, Not a Personal Diary

The biggest mistake aspiring talent make on Instagram is treating it like a personal social feed. Random selfies, nights out, memes, and personal opinions all have a place — but not on a profile you're using to attract industry attention.

Think of your Instagram as a moving portfolio. Every post should reflect who you are as a talent. That doesn't mean everything needs to be a professional shoot — authenticity is valued — but there should be a clear, consistent thread that tells a visitor what you're about.

## Lead With Your Best Images

The first nine posts on your grid are what most people see when they land on your profile. Make sure they represent you at your best. Strong headshots, clean lifestyle images, and any professional work you've done should be front and centre.

## Write a Clear Bio

Your bio should tell anyone who visits exactly who you are and what you do. Include your location, your area of work (model, actor, commercial talent), and contact details or a link to your agency profile if you have one. Keep it short and specific.

## Use Relevant Hashtags — But Don't Overdo It

Hashtags help your posts get discovered by people searching for talent. Tags like #UKModel, #LondonTalent, #CommercialModel, and #ActorsOfInstagram can put your posts in front of the right eyes. But don't spam every post with fifty irrelevant tags — it looks unprofessional.

## Engage With the Industry

Follow casting directors, agencies, photographers, and brands you'd like to work with. Comment genuinely on their posts. Build a presence in the industry online the same way you'd build it in person — by showing up consistently and professionally.

## Consistency Matters More Than Volume

You don't need to post every day. You do need to post regularly. A profile that hasn't been updated in months suggests someone who isn't active or serious. Aim for two to three posts a week at a minimum.

title: A Parent's Guide to Child and Teen Modelling
excerpt: If your child has been told they have potential, or if they've expressed an interest in modelling or acting, here's what every parent needs to know before taking the next step.
content:
If your child has been told they have potential, or if they've expressed an interest in modelling or acting, here's what every parent needs to know before taking the next step.

## Start With Your Child's Interest, Not Yours

The most important question to ask is whether your child genuinely wants to do this. Children who are pushed into modelling or acting by parents who are more enthusiastic than they are rarely thrive — and the experience can be damaging to their confidence.

If the interest is genuinely theirs, that's a strong foundation. If it isn't, no amount of talent will make the process enjoyable or sustainable.

## Understand What the Work Actually Involves

Child and teen modelling typically includes commercial advertising, catalogue work, TV commercials, and occasionally editorial shoots. The work is often sporadic, requires travel, and involves long periods of waiting on set. It can be exciting, but it is also genuinely tiring — particularly for younger children.

Make sure your child understands what a booking day actually looks like before committing to anything.

## Know the Legal Protections

In the UK, strict rules govern the employment of children in modelling and acting. Children under school leaving age require a performance licence from their local authority for most paid work. There are also rules around working hours, rest periods, and the requirement for a chaperone on set.

Any reputable agency or production will be fully aware of and compliant with these rules. If anyone suggests cutting corners, walk away.

## Watch Out for Upfront Fees

This is the single most important red flag to know: legitimate talent agencies do not charge parents upfront fees to represent their child. They do not require you to buy a photo package, pay for training, or register with a fee as a condition of signing.

Agencies earn their money by taking a commission on work they actually secure for your child. If money is being asked for before any work has been done, something is wrong.

## Keep It in Perspective

Even if your child is signed to a reputable agency, bookings are not guaranteed. Many children are represented for months before their first job. This is completely normal. The industry is competitive and highly dependent on specific briefs.

Make sure your child's self-worth is never tied to their booking rate.

title: Do Actors Need a Showreel? Here's the Honest Answer
excerpt: If you're an actor trying to get representation or break into screen work, you've probably been told you need a showreel. But do you — and if so, what should it actually contain?
content:
If you're an actor trying to get representation or break into screen work, you've probably been told you need a showreel. But the advice around showreels can be confusing — and sometimes counterproductive. Here's the honest answer.

## What Is a Showreel?

A showreel is a short video — typically two to three minutes — that showcases your on-screen performance. It's the video equivalent of a portfolio, and it's one of the primary ways casting directors and agents assess screen actors.

## Do You Actually Need One?

For screen acting work — commercials, TV, film — yes, a showreel is increasingly expected. Many casting directors will look for one when reviewing your profile. An actor without a showreel is harder to assess than one with footage to watch.

That said, a bad showreel is worse than no showreel. Poor quality footage, weak performances, or scenes that don't show you at your best will actively damage your chances. If what you have isn't good, don't use it.

## What Should Go In It?

Your best material, in the right order. The opening thirty seconds are the most important — lead with your strongest scene. Casting directors make quick decisions and may not watch to the end.

Include scenes that show range — different emotions, different character types if possible. Each clip should be short; thirty to sixty seconds per scene is generally enough. Two or three strong scenes will always outperform a reel padded with weaker material.

## What If You Have No Professional Credits?

This is where many new actors get stuck — and where some showreel companies prey on that vulnerability by charging significant fees for specially-made scenes.

The honest answer is: if you have no footage, don't manufacture a showreel just to have one. Instead, focus on building credits through short films, student productions, fringe theatre, and community projects. These are legitimate ways to generate real footage at low or no cost.

When you have something genuinely good, use it. Until then, a well-prepared headshot and a strong in-person audition can do more for you than a poor showreel.

## Technical Quality Matters

Your showreel should be properly edited, with clean audio and good picture quality. It should begin with a title card showing your name. It should be hosted somewhere accessible — Spotlight, Vimeo, or a personal website — so it can be shared easily with a link.

If your footage is good but the editing is poor, invest in a professional edit. Editing a showreel is relatively inexpensive and makes a significant difference to how the material is received.

title: What Casting Directors Wish Every Actor Knew Before Walking In
excerpt: Some of the UK and US's most respected casting directors have spoken openly about what they look for — and what consistently lets talent down. Here's what they've said.
content:
Some of the UK and US's most respected casting directors have spoken openly at industry events and in interviews about what they look for — and what consistently lets talent down. Here's what they've said.

## "Be the Person, Not the Performance" — Nina Gold

Nina Gold, one of the UK's most celebrated casting directors — responsible for The Crown, Game of Thrones, and multiple Star Wars films — has spoken publicly about the difference between actors who perform and actors who simply are.

Her consistent message: the talent who get cast are those who come in and exist truthfully in the room. They're not trying to impress. They're not performing a version of what they think she wants to see. They walk in as themselves, and they let the material do the work.

This is a harder thing to do than it sounds. Most actors arrive at auditions trying to get something — the job, the approval, the callback. The ones who succeed have usually found a way to let go of that need and just be present.

## "Arrive Knowing Exactly Who You Are" — Andy Pryor

Andy Pryor, best known for casting Doctor Who, Peaky Blinders, and Years and Years, has spoken about the importance of self-knowledge. Talent who have a clear sense of their own type, their own range, and their own strengths are far easier to cast than those who try to be everything.

He has noted that actors who come in trying to play the widest possible range often end up playing nothing convincingly. The actor who knows exactly what they do well — and does it with confidence — is the one who gets remembered.

## "The Waiting Room Is Part of the Audition" — Fiona Weir

Fiona Weir, whose credits include the Harry Potter films and Les Misérables, has made clear in interviews that how talent conducts themselves before they're called in matters. Rudeness to a runner, a sour expression in the corridor, or a dismissive attitude toward other talent does not go unnoticed.

The audition begins the moment you arrive at the building. The casting team sees everything.

## "Preparation Is Respect" — Widely Attributed

Across dozens of industry panels and interviews, casting directors repeat one message more than any other: come prepared. Know the material. Understand the brief. Have an opinion about the character or the scene.

Showing up underprepared sends a clear message that you don't take the opportunity seriously. In a competitive industry where many talented people are fighting for the same roles, that attitude is rarely forgiven twice.

## What This Means for You

The advice from the people who actually make casting decisions is strikingly consistent: be yourself, know yourself, respect the process, and prepare properly.

At Next Stage Talent, we brief every talent we submit before they go into a room. They know the brief, they know what's expected, and they're prepared to make the most of the opportunity.

title: UK Casting Directors on Self-Tapes: What They Actually Want to See
excerpt: With self-tapes now the standard first step in commercial and screen casting, we've pulled together advice shared publicly by UK casting professionals on exactly what they're looking for — and what's letting talent down.
content:
With self-tapes now the standard first step in commercial and screen casting across the UK, the advice from casting professionals has never been more consistent — or more ignored. Here's what they're actually saying.

## "Stop Trying to Be Impressive"

This is perhaps the most counterintuitive piece of advice to come from the casting community around self-tapes, and it appears repeatedly.

Casting directors — including those working in commercial and TV casting across the UK — have noted that the self-tapes they remember are rarely the ones that look the most produced or the most technically polished. They're the ones where the actor simply connected with the material and behaved naturally.

Over-produced self-tapes, elaborate locations, dramatic music, and flashy editing do not help. They suggest that the actor is trying to compensate for a performance rather than trusting it.

## "The First Ten Seconds Decide It"

Multiple casting directors have spoken publicly about how quickly they assess a self-tape. Many have confirmed that within ten seconds of the tape starting, they have a strong sense of whether this person is worth watching further.

This means your opening moments are critical. How you hold yourself. How you take a breath before you begin. Whether you seem comfortable or tense. All of that reads before you've delivered a single line.

## "Sound Quality Is Non-Negotiable"

If there is one technical note that comes up more than any other in casting director feedback on self-tapes, it is audio. Poor sound quality — muffled voices, echo, background noise — is cited again and again as a reason to stop watching.

UK casting professionals have been explicit about this in panel discussions: they can overlook imperfect lighting far more readily than they can overlook poor audio. If the performance can't be heard clearly, the tape is unusable.

## "Read the Brief. Then Read It Again."

One of the most common frustrations expressed by casting directors reviewing commercial self-tapes is talent who clearly haven't read — or haven't followed — the brief they were given.

If the brief asks for a natural, low-key delivery and the tape comes back as a full theatrical performance, that's not just a wrong choice. It tells the casting director that this person either can't follow direction or doesn't bother to try.

## "We Are Not Looking for Perfection"

Casting director Lucy Bevan, whose work spans major UK and international productions, has spoken about the tendency for actors to over-edit their self-tapes — selecting only the most technically perfect take rather than the most alive one.

The take where something unexpected happened. Where there was a genuine moment of connection with the reader. Where the actor was slightly off-script but completely present. These are often more interesting than a word-perfect but lifeless performance.

title: Self-Tape Auditions in 2026: How to Stand Out Before You Even Enter the Room
excerpt: self-tape-auditions-2026
content:
The self-tape has gone from emergency workaround to industry standard — and it's not going anywhere. Casting directors at major UK agencies now report receiving upwards of 400 self-tapes per role. The question is no longer whether you can self-tape. It's whether yours gets watched past the first ten seconds.

## The Setup Still Matters (Even at Home)

You don't need a studio. You do need a clean, neutral background — a plain wall beats a busy bookshelf every time. Ring lights are affordable and make an enormous difference to how professional your tape looks. Position the camera at eye level, never below. A slightly warm, well-lit face reads as confident. A dark, shadowy frame reads as unprepared — regardless of how good the performance is.

## Slating: First Impressions Are Everything

Your slate — name, age, and agency — sets the tone before you've said a single line. Keep it natural, keep it brief, and look directly into the lens. Casting director Shaheen Baig, whose credits include Normal People and The Pursuit of Love, has spoken publicly about how a warm, direct slate can make a casting director immediately want to watch more. Think of it as your handshake.

## Nail the Technical Basics

Poor audio ruins a great performance faster than anything else. If you're filming on a phone, an inexpensive lapel mic will transform your sound quality. Film horizontally for drama, and always check the aspect ratio matches what the brief specifies. Submitting a vertical tape for a TV drama brief signals that you haven't read the brief — which is the last impression you want to leave.

## One Take or Many?

Submit your best take, not your first. That said, avoid over-rehearsing yourself into a polished, hollow performance. The performances that get callbacks tend to feel alive and responsive — as if something real is happening, not as if lines are being delivered. Record multiple takes, step away, then come back and watch them with fresh eyes.

## What Casting Directors Are Actually Looking For

Beyond technical quality, casting directors are reading your tape for instinct, presence, and specificity. Playing a choice — even the "wrong" choice — is usually more interesting than a safe, generalised read. Show them something. Take a risk. A tape that's interesting and imperfect will beat a technically perfect tape that says nothing every time.
